To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the new health promotion payment was not associated with a substantial change in clinical practice; 2) general practitioners did not raise the issue of smoking more frequently in response to the new payment; and 3) health professionals were strongly negative about this payment.

general practitioners and practice nurses in Leicester did not substantially change their clinical practice or the way in which their practice was organized to claim a pilot payment aimed at encouraging general practitioners to give antismoking advice.

1) general practitioners did not substantially change their practice in order to claim a pilot payment aimed at encouraging antismoking advice; 2) the new health promotion payment was strongly disliked by general practitioners and practice nurses; 3) the new health payment did not overcome resistance towards raising the topic of antismoking advice in consultations.

the introduction of a payment to general practitioners and practice nurses for giving antismoking advice.
how the introduction of a new payment for health promotion activity affected the way in which general practitioners and practice nurses worked in their general practices.
the impact of financial incentives for general practitioners on smoking cessation advice.

the payment did not work.
